Across difficulty levels, 0 to 67% of one-shot kernels pass the correctness tests, and only 0 to 36% are both correct and faster than baselines (@fig-ch05-kernel-funnel). The difference separates producing a candidate from passing its behavioral checks, and passing those checks from improving performance.

This drop-off changes how generative methods should be compared. Reporting only the best generated kernel omits discarded drafts, compilation, and repair. It also leaves open whether a conventional autotuner could have found a better implementation with the same resources. @tbl-generation-construction-pair describes a prospective HLS comparison that addresses those questions: the constructors differ, while the input problem, tool flow, and resource allowances are matched. This is a proposed evaluation plan, separate from the reported KernelBench results.

| **Aspect** | **Prospective matched-construction comparison** |
| --- | --- |
| **Artifact and semantics** | Pin executable C/C++ compute kernel, target FPGA device and speed grade, clock, numerical tolerance, and Vitis HLS version before selecting constructors. |
| **Construction arms** | Predeclare strongest practical conventional HLS autotuner (Tcl pragma search or solver design-space exploration (DSE)) and one code-generating model. Both receive identical kernels and tool feedback. |
| **Shared tools and checks** | Both paths use the same Vitis HLS flow, C-simulation, C/RTL co-simulation, and Vivado synthesis, implementation, and timing checks for the target FPGA. |
| **Matched resources** | Pin context limits, wall-clock budgets, synthesis allowances, and expert setup allowances. |
| **Recorded result** | Retain attempted artifacts, synthesis failures, latency/initiation interval (II) metrics, resource utilization, tool costs, elapsed time, and expert hours. |
: **A generation comparison must match construction paths, not only final artifacts.** Matched conditions ensure conventional autotuners and generative models compete fairly. {#tbl-generation-construction-pair tbl-colwidths="[24,76]"}

Chip-Chat demonstrates interactive RTL generation in which language models drafted Verilog for an 8-bit processor, with human revision and tool feedback contributing to the path to tapeout [@BlockloveEtAl2023ChipChat]. This connects generation to an iterative process: a returned error or implementation result becomes information for the next proposal. Checks can also occur during construction. An illustrative Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) over AST edits could examine partial candidates with linters and unit assertions, rejecting a port-width or type defect before expanding dependent code. Choosing which partial candidate to expand introduces optimization into the generative process.

Multi-agent debate supplies another organizational idea [@DuEtAl2024MultiagentDebate]. In an illustrative hardware workflow, separate agents could draft RTL, inspect lint and clock-domain crossing (CDC) reports, write tests, and propose formal properties. These distinct assignments make responsibilities visible, but they do not prevent the agents from sharing a specification error. Independence has to come from the checking mechanism: separately derived properties, reference behavior, or tool observations capable of exposing the disputed assumption. A second agent's agreement alone does not establish it.

Generation, tree search, and agent coordination provide ways to construct and revise candidates. The checks determine which artifacts satisfy the required properties. Even if construction reliably produces valid candidates, the study may have too many alternatives to evaluate. It then needs a search policy that decides where to spend the remaining tool budget.

## Search Tactics and Budget Allocation {#sec-search-tactics-budget-allocation}

Once candidates can be constructed and evaluated, search must decide where to spend the next evaluation. For the Lighthouse datapath, one option is to refine an organization that has already performed well. Another is to examine a different organization whose behavior is less certain. The first is exploitation: using what the study has learned to pursue improvement. The second is exploration: gathering information that may reveal a better alternative. A limited tool budget makes the balance consequential, because time spent on one candidate is unavailable for another.

A surrogate-guided search makes this balance explicit through an *acquisition function*, a rule that scores possible evaluations using predictions and their uncertainty. The predictor estimates what a candidate may achieve; the acquisition function expresses why evaluating it would be useful. Bayesian optimization repeats this process: fit or update a surrogate, select an evaluation using the acquisition rule, obtain a tool result, and use that observation to guide the next choice.

For a quantity being maximized, an upper-confidence-bound acquisition rule scores a candidate using $\mu(x)+\kappa\sigma(x)$. Here $\mu(x)$ is the surrogate's predicted mean, $\sigma(x)$ its predictive standard deviation, and $\kappa$ the weight assigned to uncertainty. A high mean favors exploitation; a large uncertainty term can make a less-tested candidate worth examining. For minimizing a cost such as energy, the corresponding optimistic direction is toward lower values. The acquisition score is a search priority, not a measured benefit or a guarantee of feasibility.

The two panels in @fig-bayesian-optimization separate prediction from selection. The upper panel shows a Gaussian-process estimate conditioned on three observations. The lower panel combines its mean and uncertainty to choose another evaluation. This one-parameter illustration explains the selection rule; it is not a measured datapath search or a claim that the parameter captures all relevant architectural choices.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-bayesian-optimization
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Bayesian optimization allocates evaluation budget by balancing exploitation and exploration.**
#|   In this illustrative one-parameter Gaussian process model, the top panel plots the surrogate mean
#|   prediction (solid blue curve) alongside an uncertainty envelope ($\pm 1\sigma$, shaded region) anchored
#|   by three observed points. The bottom panel plots the upper-confidence-bound acquisition function
#|   ($\mu(x) + \kappa \sigma(x)$), which selects the next candidate evaluation point by trading off
#|   high predicted mean (exploitation) against wide predictive uncertainty (exploration). All values are illustrative.
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Two stacked panels over a shared design-space axis. Top: a surrogate mean curve, a shaded uncertainty band, and three observation points. Bottom: an acquisition curve labeled at an exploit region, with an arrow marking the next evaluation as the combination of mean and uncertainty."

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

# Illustrative 1-D Gaussian-process posterior with a radial-basis-function
# kernel and a small observation-noise term. Deterministic, with no random
# sampling. The acquisition is an upper-confidence bound (mean + 1.6 sigma).
apply_style()

def rbf_kernel(a, b, length_scale=1.35):
    return np.exp(-0.5 * ((a[:, None] - b[None, :]) / length_scale) ** 2)

x = np.linspace(0, 10, 400)
x_obs = np.array([1.2, 3.8, 7.2])
y_obs = np.array([0.28, 1.03, -0.48])

noise_variance = 0.0025
k_obs = rbf_kernel(x_obs, x_obs) + noise_variance * np.eye(len(x_obs))
k_cross = rbf_kernel(x_obs, x)
alpha = np.linalg.solve(k_obs, y_obs)
mean = k_cross.T @ alpha
posterior_covariance = rbf_kernel(x, x) - k_cross.T @ np.linalg.solve(k_obs, k_cross)
sigma = np.sqrt(np.clip(np.diag(posterior_covariance), 0.0, None))
kappa = 1.6
acq = mean + kappa * sigma

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(
    2, 1, figsize=(5.2, 3.5), sharex=True, gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [2.1, 1]}
)

ax1.fill_between(x, mean - sigma, mean + sigma, color=COLORS["workload"],
                 alpha=0.15, linewidth=0, label="Uncertainty")
ax1.plot(x, mean, color=COLORS["workload"], linewidth=1.8, label="Surrogate mean")
ax1.scatter(x_obs, y_obs, s=34, marker="o", facecolor=COLORS["evidence"],
            edgecolor=COLORS["evidence_ink"], linewidth=1.0, zorder=4,
            label="Observations")
ax1.set_ylabel("Objective", fontsize=6.8)
ax1.tick_params(labelsize=6.0)
ax1.legend(loc="upper right", frameon=False, fontsize=5.8, handlelength=1.4,
           borderaxespad=0.2, labelspacing=0.35)
ax1.margins(y=0.18)

ax2.fill_between(x, acq.min() - 0.05, acq, color=COLORS["methods"],
                 alpha=0.18, linewidth=0)
ax2.plot(x, acq, color=COLORS["methods"], linewidth=1.7)
x_next = float(x[int(np.argmax(acq))])
ax2.scatter([x_next], [acq.max()], s=30, marker="s", facecolor=COLORS["methods"],
            edgecolor=COLORS["methods_ink"], linewidth=1.0, zorder=4)
ax2.text(3.8, acq.max() * 0.60, "Exploit\n(high mean)", ha="center",
            fontsize=5.6, color=COLORS["methods_ink"], fontweight="bold",
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", alpha=0.9))
ax2.annotate("Next evaluation\n(mean + uncertainty)", xy=(x_next, acq.max()),
             xytext=(1.2, acq.max() * 0.42), ha="center", fontsize=5.6,
             color=COLORS["methods_ink"], fontweight="bold",
             bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.2", facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", alpha=0.9),
             arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", color=COLORS["methods_ink"], lw=0.8))
ax2.set_ylabel("Acquisition", fontsize=6.8)
ax2.set_xlabel("Design space (one parameter)", fontsize=6.8)
ax2.tick_params(labelsize=6.0)
ax2.set_yticks([])

fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.10, right=0.98, top=0.98, bottom=0.11, hspace=0.12)
```

The selected point need not have the highest predicted mean: uncertainty can justify spending an evaluation there. Other acquisition rules target expected improvement or information gain. The choice depends on what the study needs to learn, the cost of the next observation, and whether the model's uncertainty is useful under the current search conditions (@sec-support-limits).

The rule must also respect the candidate space. When a parameter is discrete, such as set associativity in $\{2,4,8,16\}$, treating it as an unrestricted continuous variable can produce an unevaluable proposal or misleading notions of similarity. Gaussian processes can use suitable input transformations or kernels; tree-based models and mixed-integer formulations provide other options. Known constraints should be enforced during construction or checked before expensive evaluation. A topology or instruction set architecture (ISA) change that cannot be expressed in the current representation requires revising that representation before the search can consider it.

Parallel tools change how evaluations are allocated. A synchronous search can choose a batch and wait for its results; an asynchronous search can request another candidate when a slot becomes free. In either case, selection should account for evaluations already in flight, so that several slots do not unknowingly repeat the same work. Deliberate repetition can still be useful for estimating noise or confirming a close comparison. The trade-off is between using available capacity and waiting for information that might improve the next choice.

Feedback must retain its meaning when it enters the search. A run stopped at a time limit provides a lower bound on its completion time, a right-censored observation [@KleinMoeschberger2003Survival]. It does not provide an ordinary measurement of energy, area, or another unfinished objective. A search may model timeout probability separately or use an explicit failure penalty, but that penalty is a selection policy rather than a measured hardware result. Infrastructure failures and nonconvergent runs likewise require distinct handling. The dataset distinctions in @sec-data-representations-world-models matter here because misencoded feedback can teach the optimizer to prefer failed evaluations.

Multi-fidelity Bayesian optimization adds a choice of evaluation fidelity to the choice of candidate [@KandasamyEtAl2017MultiFidelityBO]. A cheaper approximation is useful when its result can inform the target comparison at lower cost; it does not replace checks of properties it cannot observe. The study must retain which approximation produced each observation and reserve enough budget for reference evaluations. These choices describe how search spends its resources. Choosing an algorithm requires examining how its mechanism carries out those decisions.

## Optimization Algorithms and Heuristics

Optimization algorithms differ in how they construct a search, use feedback, and retain information across evaluations. Method comparisons depend on the problem, representation, and experimental conditions [@HendersonEtAl2018DeepRL; @KrishnanEtAl2023ArchGym]. For the Lighthouse datapath, a search over a few supplied implementations differs from a search over arithmetic graphs or a sequence of structural edits. Understanding those differences helps identify which mechanisms are worth comparing.

Enumeration evaluates every member of a finite candidate set. It resolves the best choice within that set when the evaluations are adequate and affordable, but its cost grows with the number of candidates. Random search samples legal candidates without using previous scores to direct later samples. It provides a transparent baseline, although its effectiveness depends on which designs the sampler makes likely. Domain heuristics instead use engineering rules to choose promising changes, such as prioritizing a transformation on a critical path.

Local search revises a current candidate and compares nearby alternatives. Simulated annealing also sometimes accepts a worse candidate, with acceptance controlled by a temperature schedule, to allow movement beyond a local optimum. Evolutionary search maintains a population, selecting candidates and producing new ones through mutation or recombination. For an arithmetic graph, these operators must preserve legality or include a repair step. The ability to explore many alternatives has to be balanced against the cost of evaluating the population.

Bayesian optimization uses the surrogate and acquisition rule described in @sec-search-tactics-budget-allocation to guide expensive evaluations. It can be useful when relatively few observations provide enough information to direct the search. Differentiable optimization uses gradients of an objective or a differentiable approximation. Discrete hardware choices require a suitable relaxation or another mapping back to legal candidates, followed by evaluation of the resulting discrete design. A good relaxed solution need not remain good after that conversion.

Mathematical programming and constraint solvers use explicit objectives and constraints to search an encoded problem. They can exploit known structure without first learning a search policy, although the encoding and solution process have their own costs. Equality saturation provides a related way to retain alternatives during rewriting.[^fn-egraph-c05] A greedy sequence of transformations can discard a form that would have enabled a better later transformation. An e-graph instead retains equivalent forms reached through supplied rewrite rules, until those rules add no new information or the search reaches its budget. An extraction pass chooses a low-cost represented netlist or schedule using a cost model and an algorithm such as integer linear programming or dynamic programming; the `egg` library provides one implementation. The rewrite rules must preserve the intended semantics, and graph growth and extraction still consume resources.

Screening experiments provide another way to reduce a search before committing to many evaluations. They estimate which factors have the largest effects [@PlackettBurman1946Design]. Their interpretation can rely on interactions being small enough not to obscure those effects. In the datapath example, pipeline depth and resource sharing may interact, so screening each factor without accounting for that dependence could discard a useful combination.

Reinforcement learning learns a policy for choosing actions from represented state using rewards from interaction. This can suit sequential problems in which earlier actions change later options, although sequential structure alone does not rule out conventional search or planning. Macro placement provides an example: placing a block changes the available space and can affect later routing choices. A policy can select placements from the partial floorplan, with feedback assessing the resulting arrangement (@fig-alphachip-placement) [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement].

![**A placement policy learns to choose actions from a partial floorplan.** In the reinforcement-learning macro placement framework [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement], the policy places macros sequentially, receiving an updated partial floorplan after each step. Once the macros are placed, an approximate standard-cell placement supports a proxy cost combining wirelength, congestion, and density; its negative supplies a terminal reward. Optimizing this reward still requires downstream checks of placement legality, routing, and timing.](images/fig-alphachip-placement){#fig-alphachip-placement width="100%" fig-alt="A loop with separate lanes for a placement policy's outbound macro-location action and the partial floorplan's inbound next state. After placing all macros, an approximate standard-cell placement precedes a density, congestion, and wirelength proxy cost, whose negative becomes the terminal reward."}

A learned placement policy has a training cost before it offers reusable action choices. If every training interaction invokes a full physical implementation flow, compute and license use may dominate the budget. Long action sequences with only a terminal reward also leave the policy with little feedback about which placement caused a failure. Intermediate proxy feedback and design-rule penalties can guide training, but their effect on the final placement still needs confirmation. Cheap proxy rewards reduce evaluation cost, while reuse across related blocks can spread training cost across decisions; transfer must be demonstrated on the blocks that will use the policy.

For a one-off architectural decision, direct search, deterministic heuristics, or Bayesian optimization may avoid a training cost that has little opportunity to be amortized. When evaluation budgets are limited, the relevant comparison is how much confirmed improvement each method reaches before that budget runs out.

A convergence curve makes the budget dependence visible: an approach can lead early and improve little thereafter, while another continues finding better candidates. The retained comparison in @fig-ch05-search-efficiency illustrates that trajectory shape over 100 evaluations. Its generating harness and score definition are missing, so the plotted percentages cannot establish a measured power, performance, and area (PPA) improvement or an empirical ranking of the named methods. The useful reading here is how a crossover changes the choice of budget horizon; it does not tell us which optimizer to deploy.

```{python}
steps = sorted(list(next(iter(records.values())).keys()))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 3.4))

bo_key = "Bayesian " + "Optimization (GP-BO)"
styles = {

        "linestyle": "-",
        "linewidth": 1.9,
        "label": "Bayesian optimization (GP-BO)",
        "zorder": 5,
        "fill_alpha": 0.16,
    },
    "Simulated Annealing": {
        "color": COLORS.get("green", "#2CA02C"),
        "linestyle": "-.",
        "linewidth": 1.6,
        "label": "Simulated Annealing",
        "zorder": 4,
        "fill_alpha": 0.12,
    },
    "Genetic Algorithm": {
        "color": COLORS["purple"],
        "linestyle": "--",
        "linewidth": 1.6,
        "label": "Genetic Algorithm",
        "zorder": 3,
        "fill_alpha": 0.14,
    },
    "Random Search": {
        "color": COLORS["muted"],
        "linestyle": ":",
        "linewidth": 1.4,
        "label": "Random Search (Baseline)",
        "zorder": 2,
        "fill_alpha": 0.10,
    },
}

for alg, cfg in styles.items():
    if alg not in records:
        continue
    means = np.array([np.mean(records[alg][s]) for s in steps])
    p25s = np.array([np.percentile(records[alg][s], 25) for s in steps])
    p75s = np.array([np.percentile(records[alg][s], 75) for s in steps])

    ax.plot(
        steps,
        means,
        color=cfg["color"],
        linestyle=cfg["linestyle"],
        linewidth=cfg["linewidth"],
        label=cfg["label"],
        zorder=cfg["zorder"],
    )
    ax.fill_between(
        steps,
        p25s,
        p75s,
        color=cfg["color"],
        alpha=cfg["fill_alpha"],
        zorder=cfg["zorder"] - 1,
    )

ax.set_xlim(1, 100)
ax.set_ylim(-20, 240)
ax.set_xlabel("Simulation budget (evaluations $N$)", fontsize=6.8)
ax.set_ylabel("Reported score gain (%)", fontsize=6.8)

ax.axhline(0, color=COLORS["muted"], linestyle="-", linewidth=0.6, alpha=0.5, zorder=1)

ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=5.4, loc="lower right")
ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=6.0, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.grid(True, color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.45, zorder=0)

for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
plt.close(fig)
```

The crossing of the curves is the lesson (@fig-ch05-search-efficiency). An early lead need not persist to the end of the available budget. To use such a comparison as evidence, an actual study must retain its objective, baseline, search implementations, and evaluation conditions, and charge setup and qualification alongside candidate evaluations. Without those records, the trajectory cannot tell us whether its apparent gain is affordable or physically meaningful.

The objective also shapes the search. For the datapath, minimizing energy subject to area and timing limits is a constrained single-objective problem. If the study instead seeks several useful trade-offs, multi-objective optimization can retain nondominated candidates: no other evaluated candidate is at least as good on every objective and strictly better on one [@Deb2001MultiObjective]. This set approximates the Pareto frontier over the designs examined; it need not be the frontier of the entire design space. A weighted score offers another formulation, but the weights encode preferences and may hide alternatives that an architect would want to compare.

The mechanisms have different prerequisites and failure modes (@tbl-optimization-methods). The table summarizes where each can be useful. These are starting points for a comparison, not categorical rules that make an algorithm valid or invalid solely from its name.

| **Search procedure** | **Strong fit** | **Required conditions** | **Common mismatch** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Enumeration | Small, finite legal spaces where every candidate is evaluable. | Explicit action space, affordable exhaustive coverage. | Applying after space exceeds available budget. |
| Random search / sampling | Large spaces permitting independent samples; transparent baseline. | Legal sampler, matched budget, retained failures. | Treating as insurance against flawed objectives. |
| Deterministic heuristics | Spaces with exploitable domain structure. | Explicit rules, assumptions, clear stopping rules. | Hiding manual tuning or biasing search away from optimal regions. |
| Simulated annealing | Spaces with useful local moves and multiple local optima. | Legal neighborhood, acceptance and temperature schedules, evaluation budget. | Moves or cooling schedules that leave little opportunity to reach better regions. |
| Bayesian optimization | Costly evaluations where a surrogate can guide selection from limited observations. | Suitable representation, useful uncertainty estimates, acquisition rule, evaluation budget. | A surrogate or acquisition rule poorly matched to the candidate space or changing feedback. |
| Differentiable optimization | Continuous parameters or trustworthy relaxations. | Useful gradients, post-discretization verification. | Ignoring discretization gaps, yielding unrealizable hardware. |
| Evolutionary search | Discrete/mixed spaces with population variation operators. | Legal mutation/crossover or repair, sufficient evaluations for the population. | Too few evaluations to improve the population or weak comparison baselines. |
| Reinforcement learning | Sequential choices where learning a policy can repay its interaction cost. | Informative state, meaningful rewards, affordable training, demonstrated reuse when needed. | Paying to train a policy for a problem that direct search resolves more cheaply. |
| Mathematical programming / solvers | Algebraic objectives, discrete choices, explicit constraints. | Formalizable objectives and constraints. | Optimizing unrepresented architectural desiderata. |
: **Search mechanisms differ in the structure and feedback they require.** Suitability depends on the candidate representation, available evaluations, and cost of fitting or tuning the procedure. {#tbl-optimization-methods tbl-colwidths="[22,26,26,26]"}

Learned optimizers must be benchmarked against simple baselines (enumeration, random search, or domain heuristics) under identical spaces and tool budgets [@BergstraBengio2012RandomSearch]. PrefixRL illustrates this discipline in arithmetic circuit synthesis by integrating logic synthesis directly into its evaluation loop [@RoyEtAl2021PrefixRL].

The toolchain's existing optimizer is another important comparator. Synthesis transformations, HLS tuning, and placement flows can incorporate extensive domain knowledge, heuristics, solvers, and other optimization techniques. Beating random search alone does not establish an advantage over those practical alternatives. Compare with an applicable, well-tuned tool flow under matched conditions, or explain why that comparison could not be performed. The useful result is the improvement attributable to the proposed method after its setup and tuning costs are included.

Choose stopping conditions before running the search. A study may stop when a candidate meets its declared improvement and feasibility criteria, when its evaluation or tool-time budget is exhausted, or when the expected value of further improvement no longer warrants another evaluation block. Charge failed and incomplete runs against the resources they consume. Meeting an acceptance criterion establishes a sufficient result for that study, not necessarily a global optimum; failing to find a feasible candidate within budget does not prove that none exists.

For the compact cache comparison, the limit remains four cycle-level runs, with earlier stopping only if the declared comparison and feasibility checks resolve the capacity decision. For the datapath, acceptance might require confirmed energy improvement while meeting throughput, area, and timing constraints. Each rule connects the search to a decision rather than to an indefinite pursuit of a better score. A broader design system can then combine that search mechanism with generation and prediction where those methods perform additional work.

## Composing Prediction, Generation, and Optimization {#sec-one-model-specialists-hybrid}

A search procedure needs candidates or actions to select, and feedback with which to compare them. Generation can construct those candidates; prediction can estimate properties that are expensive to evaluate. Composing these methods is useful when their contributions improve the study together. It does not require every study to use all three families.

Consider an illustrative redesign of the Lighthouse arithmetic datapath. A generator proposes a different arithmetic organization or pipeline structure, subject to the specified computation and interface requirements. After initial structural and functional checks, a supported surrogate estimates area and delay. An optimizer uses those estimates, previous evaluation results, and the remaining budget to select which candidate should receive a more expensive implementation evaluation. Energy, area, and timing results then inform the next selection or request for revision. The generator supplies alternatives, the predictor estimates consequences, and the optimizer directs the search toward the objective.

The feedback determines whether the combination works. A timing failure may motivate a revised pipeline structure; a large prediction error may instead require evaluating similar candidates directly or updating the surrogate before relying on it again. Newly generated structures can fall outside the predictor's supported representations even when they are functionally correct. The components therefore need to share the candidate's identity and evaluation conditions, while distinguishing predicted properties from checked results. This is a possible design loop, not a report of an executed Lighthouse experiment.

The roles need not correspond to separate models or occur once in a fixed order. An evolutionary procedure, for example, can both construct variants and select among them. A neural generator can also work with symbolic solvers or static compiler passes that enforce encoded constraints. AutoTVM and Ansor provide concrete examples of composing search and learned cost models for tensor programs [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM; @ZhengEtAl2020Ansor]. Their compositions serve their particular search problems; they do not establish a universal sequence for architecture design.

As a loop grows, it may also need repair, diagnosis, and coordination. The distinctions in @tbl-method-role-handoffs specify what each job produces and how another component can use it. They describe responsibilities that a human, a conventional tool, or a learned component might perform.

| **Engineering role** | **Concrete output** | **Next check or handoff** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Proposal** | Named candidate or experiment request with identified changes. | Verify legality and scope before invoking expensive tools. |
| **Screening** | Scoped estimate or ranking with predicted properties and uncertainty. | Route selected candidates to measurement path; retain predictions for qualification. |
| **Search** | Next candidate or experiment, selection basis, remaining budget. | Execute within the current search formulation; make any proposed change to that formulation explicit. |
| **Static Analysis** | Testable defect, missing assumption, or conflict tied to named artifact. | Use the finding to guide revision; check whether the revised candidate resolves it. |
| **Repair** | Revised artifact linked to parent and modification record. | Treat as fresh candidate; rerun affected checks. |
| **Checking** | Result from named check under declared conditions (including timeouts/failures). | Interpret what the check establishes and what remains untested (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). |
| **Diagnostic Localization** | Proposed mechanism and distinguishing contrast conditions. | Request targeted measurement; analysis does not substitute for verification. |
| **Coordination** | Ordered request graph with dependencies, budgets, and artifact IDs. | Hand requests to environment for tool orchestration. |
: **Each engineering role produces an output that another role can use.** Separating proposals, estimates, revisions, and checked results makes their different contributions explicit. {#tbl-method-role-handoffs tbl-colwidths="[20,38,42]"}

The repair row illustrates why these distinctions matter. A revised datapath is a new candidate: the earlier timing result belongs to its parent and cannot be carried forward as if no design change occurred. Likewise, a diagnosis suggests what to investigate, while a targeted check tests that explanation. A component can perform several roles, but its outputs still need to preserve these differences.

We can simplify the datapath loop by asking which work is actually needed. If a few candidate implementations already exist and direct evaluation is affordable, neither generation nor a learned screen may be necessary. If candidate construction is needed but each design is cheap to evaluate, generation and optimization can use direct feedback. If evaluations take days, prediction becomes attractive only when suitable data and sufficient accuracy allow it to save more evaluation work than it adds in fitting and qualification.

These alternatives lead to different compositions (@tbl-method-organization). Here, “generation only” means generation is the only added method family; compilation, checking, and evaluation are still required. The same convention applies to the other rows. The choice concerns which methods improve the work, not which essential engineering checks can be omitted.

| **Composition** | **When justified** | **What must be established** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Direct tools / conventional technique | Analytical models, solvers, or direct simulations perform work economically. | Retain unless an added component improves result quality or total cost while preserving checks. |
| Generation only | New or revised artifacts are needed; direct checking is affordable. | Generated candidates meet the intended requirements at an acceptable construction and checking cost. |
| Prediction only | Candidates require cheap screening before expensive simulation. | Retain predictor only while qualification and confirmation cost less than direct evaluation. |
| Optimization only | Selecting among existing candidates or legal actions requires a search. | Benchmark against simple baselines; stop when further search yields diminishing returns. |
| Generation + prediction | Candidate construction and cheap screening are useful before expensive evaluation. | Predictor has support for the generated structures; selected candidates receive the required confirmation. |
| Generation + optimization | Candidate construction required under selective search budget without supported surrogate. | Optimizer uses direct tool feedback; generated candidates pass verification. |
| Prediction + optimization | Surrogate enables selective search under expensive tool feedback. | Keep surrogate, acquisition rule, and confirmation stages separately inspectable. |
| Generation + prediction + optimization | Constructing alternatives, estimating consequences, and directing search each improve the study. | Their combined benefit exceeds fitting, integration, and checking costs at the required result quality. |
: **Pipeline components must earn their cost in the declared study.** Each composition addresses particular work and introduces qualification, integration, and checking costs. The comparison is against a credible simpler path at the required result quality. {#tbl-method-organization tbl-colwidths="[24,34,42]"}

The generation-plus-optimization row fits a datapath search that constructs alternatives and evaluates them directly. Adding prediction is a separate decision, justified only if the screen improves that search at the available budget. The rows therefore describe alternatives rather than a progression toward an ideal three-component system. The compiler and cache studies apply this reasoning to two different candidate spaces and evaluation costs.

## Method Selection in Two Contrasting Studies

Two studies can both aim to select a better implementation and still need different methods. Tensor-program tuning may involve more schedules than can be measured on the target hardware, while the prospective mobile system-on-chip (SoC) cache study compares only three capacities. Their contrast makes method selection concrete: how many alternatives need evaluation, where will useful observations come from, and what can the budget cover?

### Compiler Tuning versus Cache Evaluation

For a fixed tensor operator and hardware target, a schedule determines implementation choices such as loop order, tiling, and parallel execution. AutoTVM combines a learned cost model with search over these choices. Selected programs run on the target hardware, and their measured runtimes supply observations for updating the model [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]. Compatible observations from earlier workloads can help, but a preexisting training dataset is not required; observations can accumulate during tuning.

The reason to learn a cost model is that relatively few measured schedules may help prioritize many unmeasured ones. That benefit must repay the measurements used to learn the model as well as fitting and inference. A large schedule space creates an opportunity for selective search, but does not by itself show that a learned model improves on conventional tuning.

The illustrative cache study instead proposes three discrete capacity settings (2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, and 4\ MiB) under a budget intended to cover direct static random-access memory (SRAM) screening and cycle-level simulation. With no matching prior data, collecting measurements to train a surrogate would consume part of the same small evaluation budget. Direct evaluation is therefore the proposed starting method (@tbl-worked-method-decisions). It still uses analytical models and simulation to estimate hardware behavior; it adds no learned surrogate. Execution remains pending.

| **Decision parameter** | **Tensor-program tuning plan** | **Illustrative cache study** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Job** | Select a schedule that improves operator runtime on the target hardware. | Compare 2\ MiB baseline against 3\ MiB and 4\ MiB without expanding scope. |
| **Inputs and support** | Fixed operator and target, legal schedules, compiler version, evaluation budget, measurements collected during tuning; compatible prior data if available. | Three proposed `l2.capacity` settings, hardware/software specifications, SRAM constraints, no prior matching data. |
| **Approach status** | Search and learned cost modeling, following the AutoTVM pattern; study-specific comparator and budget still required. | Analytical SRAM screening followed by matched cycle-level simulations of the supplied candidates; no added generator or learned surrogate. |
| **Output and legal actions** | Selected legal schedule with checked correctness and measured target runtime. | Modeled SRAM metrics and matched cycle-level simulation results for 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, or 4\ MiB only. |
| **Evaluator and checks** | Compile and check outputs against the operator specification; measure runtime under matched target conditions. | SRAM physical model checks limits; cycle-level simulation and power models return system metrics. |
| **Feedback cost** | Surrogate fitting, candidate compilation, target runs, tuning review. | Three SRAM evaluations, maximum four cycle-level runs. |
| **Fallback and stop** | Compare with an applicable default schedule or tuned operator implementation; set the measurement budget and stopping criteria. | If SRAM screening is unavailable, simulate performance while keeping physical feasibility unresolved. Stop at the declared decision or budget limit. |
: **Candidate space, available data, and feedback cost distinguish the method choices.** A large compiler schedule space can justify surrogate-guided search, whereas the proposed three-capacity cache comparison favors direct evaluation. The compiler plan draws on a published method; this comparison reports no new execution results. {#tbl-worked-method-decisions tbl-colwidths="[22,39,39]"}

The inputs and feedback-cost rows explain the contrast. In the compiler study, observations collected from some schedules can guide selection among many others. In the three-capacity cache study, obtaining training observations may already perform much of the direct comparison. The choice follows how much useful work remains after collecting the data. If the cache question expanded to many interacting design choices, or a suitable surrogate already existed, that reasoning would need to be revisited. For the current question, the evaluation plan must specify how the three capacities will be compared and what the results can establish.

### Evaluation Plan

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="Lighthouse Cache Evaluation Plan"}
**Context.** The question is whether increasing cache capacity from 2\ MiB to 3\ MiB or 4\ MiB reduces frame time while meeting the subsystem's power limit and the cache's area and access-time limits.

**Application.** Evaluate the supplied capacities directly. First assess each cache organization with an analytical SRAM model, then compare candidates through matched cycle-level simulations. No learned surrogate is proposed for this small comparison.

**Outcome.** This is an evaluation plan, not an executed result. The physical models and simulator configuration still need to be established before the plan can determine feasibility or a preferred capacity.
:::

The plan must connect a capacity setting to the hardware it represents. A larger cache may reduce misses, but it also changes storage area, leakage, and potentially access latency. Holding the workload and unrelated design choices fixed makes the comparison interpretable; holding these capacity-dependent consequences fixed would hide part of the trade-off. Each setting therefore needs a corresponding organization and a consistent rule for deriving its modeled properties.

The proposed limits in @tbl-lighthouse-approach-decision make that comparison specific. TSMC N3E is the chosen implementation target, not an available, validated technology model. Before relying on an SRAM estimate, the study must establish that its model and parameters support the target process and candidate organizations.

| **Plan detail** | **Lighthouse cache comparison** |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Selected approach** | Direct evaluation with no added learned components. |
| **Allowed change** | Vary only `l2.capacity` among 2\ MiB, 3\ MiB, and 4\ MiB. Hold workload, software, and unrelated microarchitectural choices fixed; derive capacity-dependent organization and timing consistently. |
| **Required tool roles** | A suitable SRAM model estimates cache macro area, access time, and leakage for the target conditions. A configured gem5 simulation provides frame-time and miss-rate estimates; compatible power models estimate subsystem power. |
| **Evaluation budget** | Three SRAM evaluations and at most four cycle-level runs, including failed or repeated attempts. This is a proposed limit, not a demonstrated sufficient budget. |
| **Feasibility checks** | Check functional behavior and candidate identity. Require modeled subsystem power at or below $3\ \text{W}$, total cache macro area at or below $1.5\ \text{mm}^2$, and access time at or below $2.5\ \text{ns}$. Physical feasibility additionally requires implementation timing and power analysis, including declared power intent. |
| **Performance comparison** | Compare frame time against the 2\ MiB baseline under matched conditions. Define how uncertainty will be assessed before execution; accept an improvement only when the resulting interval for baseline minus candidate frame time is positive. |
| **Fallback and stopping** | If SRAM screening is unavailable, simulation can still compare performance under explicit cache assumptions, but physical feasibility remains unresolved. Stop when the declared comparison is resolved or the budget is exhausted; report an inconclusive result if the available evidence does not separate the candidates. |
: **Direct evaluation gives the proposed cache comparison a concrete starting plan.** The small candidate set motivates the method choice, while the listed models, checks, and budget identify what must be established before a result can support that choice. {#tbl-lighthouse-approach-decision tbl-colwidths="[26,74]"}

The budget row deserves particular attention. Comparing three capacities leaves little room within four runs for failures, repeated baselines, or additional workload observations. A run count alone does not establish the uncertainty of a frame-time difference. If the planned observations cannot distinguish a candidate's improvement from the uncertainty in the comparison, the study must remain inconclusive or obtain a revised budget. Exhausting the budget does not make the lowest observed frame time a reliable winner.

This is the fixed design path introduced in @sec-architecture-20-ontology. Results select among supplied capacities rather than generate a revised organization. That scope is sufficient for the question being asked. The later worked study examines the physical definitions and tool setup still needed to execute this plan (@sec-running-the-loop).

Total cost also extends beyond the evaluations themselves (@tbl-method-role-limits). Configuring gem5, establishing the cache and power models, obtaining applicable licenses, and reviewing results all consume resources. Adding a surrogate would require data collection and qualification on top of that work. For the current three-candidate comparison, the plan identifies no expected saving that warrants those additions. Across broader studies, estimating when such additions will repay their cost remains an open methods question.

## Open Questions

The examples identify the costs that a method comparison must include. How to predict those costs and benefits before committing a limited evaluation budget leaves five questions unresolved:

- **When should analytical modeling give way to learned prediction or search?** Roofline models, Little's law, and queueing approximations may settle a decision cheaply, but their usefulness depends on whether they expose the interactions controlling that decision. Cache thrashing under multi-phase irregular traces and wire congestion during placement can make an analytical approximation too coarse. Learned residual models or search may improve the comparison, at the cost of data and qualification. The open problem is to identify this boundary from decision margins, observed model error, and remaining budget, rather than treating either analytical sufficiency or high dimensionality as a complete method-selection rule.

- **How much of a surrogate-predicted gain survives confirmation?** Search can favor positive surrogate error, especially when it enters poorly characterized regions, as the reorder-buffer hypothetical of @sec-support-limits shows. Shrinkage and calibrated intervals address different parts of this uncertainty, but neither establishes omitted physical properties. Studies need to compare frozen predictions with reference returns across candidate-pool sizes and selection policies, while detecting departures from qualified support.[^fn-ood-c05] The unresolved question is how reliably these corrections can ration expensive confirmation while retaining the candidates that would survive it.

- **How does grammar-constrained decoding affect the variety of useful candidates?** Enforcing a grammar establishes syntactic membership; it does not establish which valid designs a generator will reach within a finite budget. The method comparison must distinguish restrictions in the grammar from the sampler's distribution over the designs it permits. The unresolved issue is whether constrained generation, post-generation repair, or a combination produces a broader set of functionally correct, competitive architectures for the same construction-and-checking cost. Answering it requires examining the resulting hardware structures as well as syntax pass rates.

- **How should search spend a fixed budget when its own improvements change the evaluation bottleneck?** The stability bound (@eq-queue-stability-bound) identifies a permissible arrival rate for given pass rates and service capacities. Throttling proposals can preserve stability, but it does not establish whether the remaining budget is better spent improving proposals, qualifying a cheaper screen, or adding downstream evaluation capacity. Pass rates and runtimes must be estimated as the candidate population changes during search. The research problem is to choose among these expenditures under that uncertainty, judging the policy by confirmed results within budget rather than by queue utilization alone.

- **When do composed methods outperform a tuned simpler workflow at matched total cost?** Each added component promises better results or lower cost (@tbl-method-organization), but also introduces qualification overhead, tool translation errors, and integration latency. A fair comparison must charge qualification runs, failed invocations, surrogate recalibration, and human repair. Repeated comparisons across workload and budget regimes are needed to determine when composition retains its advantage over a well-tuned simpler workflow.

## Summary

Method selection begins by identifying the work that limits the architecture study. Roles, method families, techniques, and compositions remain distinct choices. A conventional method may already resolve the question; an added model may instead improve the result or make a comparable result cheaper. Generation can construct an alternative organization for evaluation and redesign, while prediction and optimization help estimate consequences and allocate evaluations. The architect's task is to compare those paths with their data, qualification, and checking costs included.

An algorithm cannot be judged apart from what it costs to run. A multi-tier pipeline that ignores its queue stability bound can turn a better generator into a longer backlog. Selection against a noisy surrogate can exaggerate a candidate's gain, while qualification and recalibration can consume the evaluations the surrogate was meant to save. These mechanisms explain why method choice depends on the whole checking path. Five takeaways follow:

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Role first, then family, then technique.** Define the engineering role (propose, screen, search, check) before selecting prediction, generation, or optimization, choosing concrete mechanisms and composing pipelines only when distinct computational jobs exist.
- **Smallest sufficient method.** Compare against direct evaluation and credible conventional methods. Added complexity earns its place through better supported results or lower total cost, with the required checks preserved.
- **Feed-forward queue stability.** Multi-stage evaluation pipelines must hold candidate arrivals under the stability bound with active generation throttling, so that downstream physical signoff queues do not collapse as upstream generator yield improves. A cheap screen widens that path only as far as its validated coverage reaches, never as far as its speed suggests.
- **Optimizer's curse and calibrated bounds.** Optimizing noisy predictions can select positive error. Preserve prediction-confirmation pairs, monitor coverage under the selection procedure, and use shrinkage only when its correction is supported; confirm finalists against the claimed property.
- **Generation and composition with independent checks.** A generated or revised organization becomes a candidate for evaluation. Separate construction and checking roles, then examine their shared assumptions. A parser, formal property, or reference implementation contributes only the evidence its mechanism can establish; another agent's agreement does not ensure independence.
:::

The selected method now has a defined job, an evaluation budget, and a checking path. Those promises become operational only when an environment preserves candidate identity, invokes the intended tools, and returns interpretable results and failures. Building that environment is the task of @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces.


[^fn-feedback-c05]: **Returning work in queueing models**: Retries and repeated evaluations add visits to tool stages. A model with returning work must include those visits in each stage's arrival rate; the one-pass product used here does not include them.



[^fn-eda-signoff-c05]: **Signoff Tools**: OpenSTA checks modeled circuit paths against declared timing constraints. UPF specifies power intent, such as voltage domains and power gating, for tools that analyze or verify it. SVA expresses properties; BMC checks them over a specified bounded execution horizon. These tools address complementary parts of an implementation claim.

[^fn-split-conformal-c05]: **Split-Conformal Prediction**: A separate calibration dataset supplies residuals used to construct prediction intervals. Exchangeability between calibration and test samples supports the stated marginal coverage; the guarantee does not apply automatically to an adaptively selected finalist.

[^fn-egraph-c05]: **E-graphs and Equality Saturation**: An e-graph (equivalence graph) compactly represents many equivalent expressions. Equality saturation applies a supplied set of rewrites while retaining earlier forms, so choosing one rewrite need not discard alternatives. It stops when the rules add no new information or a resource limit is reached; it does not enumerate every possible equivalent expression.


[^fn-roofline-c05]: **Analytical Roofline Models**: A visual model that bounds theoretical peak compute performance and memory bandwidth to quickly identify whether a workload will bottleneck on processing power or memory access.

[^fn-ood-c05]: **Out-of-Distribution (OOD) Detection**: Statistical tests or model scores flag inputs that differ from a reference distribution. Such detectors can support escalation, but their false alarms and missed shifts need evaluation; a lack of alarms does not establish that conformal coverage assumptions hold.

[^fn-kernelbench-c05]: **KernelBench Hardware Dependency**: Metrics like "correct and faster than eager" depend heavily on the underlying hardware (e.g., NVIDIA L40S or H100) and the specific compiler stack.

[^fn-ir-drop-c05]: **IR Drop**: A localized decrease in voltage within a chip's power distribution network caused by the resistance (R) of the wires and the current (I) drawn by switching transistors.

[^fn-sta-c05]: **Static timing analysis (STA)**: Analysis of circuit paths and modeled delays against timing constraints without simulating the circuit's full sequence of operations.

[^fn-bmc-c05]: **Bounded model checking (BMC)**: A formal technique that unrolls a sequential circuit for a fixed number of steps and checks an encoded property within that horizon. A successful bounded check alone does not prove the property for all execution lengths.
